Imagine the Earth's oceans as a giant cake. Countries that have coastlines get to claim the slices closest to them — they own those waters, control them, and make the rules there. But the vast middle of the cake? Nobody owns it. No country, no king, no government. That unclaimed, unowned expanse of ocean is called the high seas.

More precisely, the high seas are the parts of the world's oceans that lie beyond the legal boundaries of any country's authority. They are international waters — open to all nations and belonging to none.
To Truly Understand It, You Need to Know the Ocean's Zones

The ocean is not just divided into "owned" and "unowned." It is split into a series of clearly defined legal zones, like rings around a bullseye. Let's start from the coastline and move outward.

1. The Baseline
Every measurement of ocean zones starts from the baseline, which is essentially the low-tide line along a country's coast. This is the legal "edge" of the land.

2. Internal Waters
The waters on the landward side of the baseline — rivers, harbours, bays, and lagoons — are called internal waters. These are treated exactly like a country's land. A foreign ship entering them without permission can be stopped, searched, or turned away.

3. The Territorial Sea (0 to 12 nautical miles)
Extending outward from the baseline for 12 nautical miles (about 22 kilometres) is the territorial sea. A country has full sovereignty here — it's essentially underwater territory. Foreign ships may pass through peacefully, but the coastal country's law applies.

4. The Contiguous Zone (12 to 24 nautical miles)
Just beyond the territorial sea lies a 12-nautical-mile buffer zone. The country doesn't fully own it, but it has the right to enforce its customs, immigration, and sanitation laws here.

5. The Exclusive Economic Zone, or EEZ (up to 200 nautical miles)
This is the big one. Stretching up to 200 nautical miles from the baseline, the EEZ gives a country exclusive rights to all the economic resources in those waters — fish, oil, gas, minerals, wind and wave energy. Other countries can sail through or fly over freely, but they cannot exploit the resources.

6. The Continental Shelf (up to 350 nautical miles, in some cases)
Beneath the ocean lies a shelf of land that gradually slopes away from the coast before dropping into the deep ocean floor. Countries have the right to exploit the natural resources on and under this seabed, sometimes extending beyond the 200-nautical-mile EEZ limit, up to 350 nautical miles.

7. The High Seas — Where All This Ends
Once you go beyond the EEZ (and in some seabed cases, the extended continental shelf), you reach international territory. The water column — the open ocean from surface to seafloor — is the high seas. No country has jurisdiction. This starts, in most cases, at the 200-nautical-mile mark from any coast.
Just How Vast Are the High Seas?

The scale is staggering. Roughly 61% of the ocean surface lies outside the jurisdiction of any country. Since oceans themselves cover about 71% of the Earth's surface, the high seas cover approximately 43% of the entire planet. It is by far the largest geographic domain on Earth, and for most of human history, it was the least governed.
A Principle Born Centuries Ago: Mare Liberum

The concept of the high seas isn't new — it goes back over four hundred years. In 1609, a Dutch jurist named Hugo Grotius wrote a revolutionary legal essay called Mare Liberum, which translates to "The Free Sea." His argument was bold and simple: the open ocean cannot be owned, because unlike land, it cannot be permanently occupied or enclosed. Everyone uses it, everyone needs it, and therefore it must remain free for all.

This idea — known as the freedom of the seas — became the bedrock of international maritime law and remains central to how the world thinks about the high seas today.
The Modern Legal Foundation: UNCLOS

Today, the high seas are governed primarily by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, universally known as UNCLOS. It was adopted in 1982 and is often called the "constitution for the oceans." It defines all the maritime zones described above, and most importantly, it codifies what the high seas are, who can use them, and what rules apply.

UNCLOS established a simple and powerful principle: the high seas are res communis — the common heritage of all humankind. They cannot be claimed, colonised, or annexed by any state.
The Six Freedoms of the High Seas

UNCLOS gives all countries — whether they have a coastline or not — equal rights to use the high seas. These are formally known as the freedoms of the high seas, and there are six of them:

Freedom of navigation. Any ship from any country can sail through the high seas without permission from anyone. A cargo ship from Bolivia (a landlocked country) has as much right to sail the mid-Pacific as the United States Navy.

Freedom of overflight. Aircraft can fly over the high seas without restriction. No country can demand a plane turn back once it's over international waters.

Freedom to lay submarine cables and pipelines. Countries and companies can lay communications cables or oil pipelines on the seabed of the high seas.

Freedom to construct artificial islands and installations. Subject to international rules, states and entities may build platforms or structures on the high seas, provided they don't interfere with the rights of others.

Freedom of fishing. Anyone can fish on the high seas. However, this freedom is heavily qualified by international agreements aimed at preventing overfishing of shared fish stocks.

Freedom of scientific research. Any country can conduct oceanographic research, biological surveys, or climate studies on the high seas.

These freedoms must all be exercised "with due regard" for the rights of other states — meaning one country's exercise of freedom cannot unreasonably block another's.
Who Makes the Rules on a Ship at Sea?

Since no country owns the high seas, who enforces the law on a ship sailing through them?

The answer is the concept of flag state jurisdiction. Every ship in the world must be registered with a country and fly that country's flag. Once a ship is on the high seas, it falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the country whose flag it flies — not the country it came from, not the country it's headed to.

If a French ship commits an offence on the high seas, France is responsible for investigating and prosecuting it. If a Panamanian-flagged vessel breaks international law, Panama is the responsible authority. This is why you'll often hear of ships registered in countries like Panama, Liberia, or the Marshall Islands — these nations have large "open registries" where ships from all over the world register, often for lower taxes and looser regulation. This is called "flags of convenience."
But There Are Exceptions: What Other Ships Can Do

Flag state jurisdiction is the rule, but not an absolute one. International law recognises several situations where a warship or naval vessel of one country may stop and inspect a foreign ship on the high seas:

Piracy. Piracy is the oldest crime of the high seas and is considered a crime against all of humanity — what lawyers call hostis humani generis, "enemy of all mankind." Any warship from any nation can pursue, board, and detain a pirate vessel anywhere on the high seas, regardless of what flag it flies.

Slave trade. Any ship reasonably suspected of being involved in transporting enslaved people may be boarded and inspected by a foreign warship.

Unauthorised broadcasting. Ships broadcasting pirate radio or television signals into other countries' territory can be stopped by any concerned state.

Stateless vessels. Ships flying no flag at all, or fraudulently flying multiple flags, have no legal protection and can be boarded by any warship.

Hot pursuit. If a coastal country's authorities chase a vessel that violated their laws within their territorial waters, they may continue that pursuit into the high seas — as long as the pursuit was never interrupted. This is called the right of hot pursuit.
The Seabed Beneath the High Seas: "The Area"

The high seas refers specifically to the water column — the open ocean from surface down to the seafloor. But what about the actual seafloor and subsoil under those waters?

That is governed separately under UNCLOS and is officially called "the Area." The Area is defined as the seabed, ocean floor, and subsoil beyond the limits of national jurisdiction. It contains rich mineral resources — including potato-shaped lumps called polymetallic nodules that are packed with cobalt, nickel, copper, and manganese, and which have attracted growing interest as the world demands more metals for electric vehicles and batteries.

The Area is managed by an international body called the International Seabed Authority (ISA), headquartered in Jamaica. Like the high seas above, the Area is considered the common heritage of mankind, meaning no country can claim exclusive ownership of it, and any benefits derived from it are supposed to be shared with humanity as a whole.
What Has Historically Been Missing: Governance Gaps

For most of the modern era, the freedom of the high seas — while essential — created a serious problem: very little accountability. Because no country was truly in charge, several damaging activities went largely unchecked:

Fishing fleets from powerful nations operated with minimal oversight, decimating fish populations. Corporations collected and patented marine genetic resources — unique biological material from deep-sea creatures that could be used to develop medicines, cosmetics, and food products — without sharing any benefits with the wider world. Pollution poured in. Deep-sea mining proposals advanced faster than any legal framework to assess their environmental impact could catch up.

Pressures mounted from shipping, overfishing, pollution, and the looming potential of deep-sea mining, even as vast areas of the deep ocean remained under-sampled and poorly understood. This lack of knowledge was particularly urgent, given that high seas ecosystems regulate climate, sequester carbon, produce oxygen, and are closely interconnected with coastal and terrestrial systems.
The Historic Turning Point: The High Seas Treaty (2023–2026)

After nearly two decades of negotiation, the world finally acted. The text was finalised during an intergovernmental conference at the UN on 4 March 2023 and adopted on 19 June 2023. The agreement is formally known as the BBNJ Agreement — Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction — but it is widely called the High Seas Treaty.

It is the first legally binding international framework dedicated to safeguarding marine life in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

On September 19, 2025, the BBNJ Agreement reached the 60 ratification threshold, and on January 17, 2026, it entered into force.

The treaty covers four major areas. First, marine genetic resources — it requires that companies and countries that collect biological material from the high seas share the benefits fairly with the rest of the world, particularly developing nations. Second, marine protected areas (MPAs) — for the first time, the world now has a legal mechanism to designate protected zones on the high seas where damaging activities can be restricted. Third, environmental impact assessments — any activity with the potential to cause significant harm to high seas ecosystems must now be evaluated before proceeding. Fourth, capacity building — wealthier nations must help developing countries gain the technology and scientific knowledge to participate meaningfully in high seas governance.

From its entry into force date, ratifying countries are legally bound by the agreement to support conservation and sustainable management of high-seas biodiversity.
Why the High Seas Matter to Everyone — Even Landlocked People

You might wonder why anyone living far from the ocean should care about the high seas. The answer is that the high seas are not a distant irrelevance — they are a fundamental life-support system for the entire planet.

The ocean absorbs roughly a quarter of all the carbon dioxide humans emit into the atmosphere, slowing climate change. It produces more than half of the oxygen we breathe, primarily through microscopic marine organisms called phytoplankton, most of which live in the high seas. The high seas regulate global temperature and weather patterns. They are the source of food for billions of people and sustain the global fishing and shipping industries that make modern trade possible. Virtually every product you buy that was made abroad crossed the high seas to reach you.
A Quick Summary to Lock It All In

The high seas are the parts of the ocean that begin beyond the 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone of any country and extend across the deep ocean — covering roughly 61% of the ocean's surface. No nation owns them. They are the common property of all humanity, governed by the principle of the freedom of the seas, codified in the 1982 UNCLOS treaty. Ships on the high seas are ruled by the laws of the country whose flag they fly. Certain universal crimes — especially piracy — override that rule and can be prosecuted by any nation. The seabed beneath the high seas, called "the Area," is separately managed by the International Seabed Authority. And as of January 17, 2026, the world's first binding treaty to specifically protect the biodiversity of the high seas — the BBNJ Agreement — is now in force, marking a new era in how humanity governs and cares for its most vast and shared domain.
